clinicalPearls: Stenosing tenosynovitis of flexor pollicis longus at the first annular (A1) pulley, causing catching, locking or triggering of the thumb interphalangeal joint on flexion and extension.
A tender palpable nodule (Notta node) is often felt over the A1 pulley at the metacarpophalangeal flexion crease of the thumb.

Adult disease is most common in middle-aged women and is associated with diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, hypothyroidism and repetitive gripping; diabetic triggering responds less well to conservative measures.

Paediatric (congenital) trigger thumb typically presents as a fixed flexion deformity of the interphalangeal joint rather than true triggering, and a proportion resolve spontaneously in early childhood.
Grading progresses from painful triggering, to demonstrable catching that self-corrects, to locking requiring passive release, and finally to a fixed contracture.
First-line management in adults is activity modification, splinting and corticosteroid injection into the flexor sheath; injection is highly effective though less so in diabetics.
Surgical A1 pulley release (open or percutaneous) is definitive for refractory or recurrent cases; the radial digital nerve to the thumb lies close to the sheath and is at risk.
Persistent triggering after apparently adequate release should raise suspicion of an incompletely divided pulley or an unrecognised trigger at a more distal site.
reference.pathophysiology: Trigger thumb arises from a size mismatch between flexor pollicis longus and the mouth of the fibro-osseous A1 pulley. Repetitive loading and shear at the pulley provoke fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and thickening of the pulley together with tenosynovial hyperplasia of the tendon, producing a localised nodule. As the thickened tendon segment is forced through the constricted pulley it catches, generating the characteristic triggering; progressive stenosis leads to locking and, ultimately, a fixed flexion contracture. Systemic conditions such as diabetes mellitus promote glycation and matrix changes that predispose to and perpetuate the stenosis.
additionalDifferentials: Thumb metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint osteoarthritis
Flexor pollicis longus tendon rupture or partial laceration
Sesamoid pathology at the thumb MCP joint
Dupuytren nodule of the thumb ray
Retained foreign body or infective flexor tenosynovitis
Congenital clasped thumb in the paediatric setting
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical from history and examination of triggering and the Notta node
Ultrasound to confirm pulley thickening, tenosynovitis or a discrete nodule in equivocal cases
Screening for diabetes mellitus in recurrent or multi-digit disease
Thyroid function assessment where clinically suggested
Plain radiographs if concomitant joint arthritis or bony pathology is suspected
Inflammatory markers and rheumatoid screen when an inflammatory arthropathy is considered
Documentation of triggering grade and interphalangeal joint range of motion
redFlags: Fixed interphalangeal flexion contracture that will not passively extend
Signs of infective flexor tenosynovitis (fusiform swelling, pain on passive extension, disproportionate tenderness)
Loss of active interphalangeal flexion suggesting tendon rupture rather than triggering
Sensory disturbance in the thumb suggesting digital nerve involvement
reference.prognosis: Generally excellent; most adults respond to corticosteroid injection and the majority of the remainder are cured by A1 pulley release, while a substantial proportion of congenital cases resolve spontaneously or after release. Diabetic patients have higher recurrence and lower injection success.
pitfalls: Injecting or releasing without recognising an associated fixed contracture that requires additional therapy or splinting
Injuring the radial digital nerve, which crosses obliquely near the thumb A1 pulley, during percutaneous release
Dividing the oblique pulley in error, which can cause flexor pollicis longus bowstringing and loss of interphalangeal flexion power
Attributing a locked thumb to triggering when the underlying problem is joint arthritis or tendon rupture
Assuming poor injection response in diabetics reflects wrong diagnosis rather than expected reduced efficacy
references: British Society for Surgery of the Hand patient and clinical guidance
management: Manage adult disease first-line with activity modification, splinting and a corticosteroid injection into the flexor sheath at the A1 pulley, which is highly effective
Refer for surgical A1 pulley release for triggering refractory to injection or a fixed interphalangeal flexion contracture
For paediatric congenital trigger thumb, observe initially as a proportion resolve spontaneously, reserving surgical release for a persistent fixed flexion deformity
Screen for and optimise associated diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism and rheumatoid arthritis
Provide hand therapy with stretching and tendon-gliding, particularly after injection or surgical release
Monitor for recurrence, which is higher in diabetic patients, and escalate to surgery when injection fails
